en: Thus have I heard: the Sakkapañha Sutta, the twenty-first discourse of the Dīgha Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans, to the east of Rājagaha, at the Indasāla Cave on Mount Vediyaka, north of the brahmin village named Ambasaṇḍā.
Now at that time, zeal arose in Sakka, lord of the devas, to see the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to Sakka, lord of the devas:
“Where, indeed, is the Blessed One dwelling now—the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One?
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, saw the Blessed One dwelling among the Magadhans to the east of Rājagaha, in the Indasāla Cave on Mount Vediyaka, north of the brahmin village named Ambasaṇḍā.
Having seen him, he addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
“Friends, this Blessed One is staying among the Magadhans, to the east of Rājagaha, in the Indasāla Cave on Mount Vediyaka, north of the brahmin village named Ambasaṇḍā.
Friends, what if we were to approach that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in order to see him?
“Very well, venerable sir,” the Tāvatiṃsa gods replied to Sakka, lord of the devas.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabba devas:
“Dear Pañcasikha, this Blessed One is staying among the Magadhans to the east of Rājagaha, in a brahmin village named Ambasaṇḍā, on Mount Vediyaka to its north, in the Indasāla Cave.
Dear Pañcasikha, what if we were to approach that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in order to see him?”
“Yes, venerable sir,” Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabba deities, replied to Sakka, lord of the devas. Taking his yellow beluva-wood lute, he approached to attend upon Sakka, lord of the devas.

Then Sakka, lord of the devas, surrounded by the Tāvatiṃsa devas and preceded by Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabba deities—just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—[disappeared from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and appeared before the Blessed One].
In this very way, having vanished among the Tāvatiṃsa gods, he reappeared on Mount Vediyaka to the north of Ambasaṇḍā, a brahmin village to the east of Rājagaha. At that time,
Mount Vediyaka and the brahmin village of Ambasaṇḍā were exceedingly radiant, as is the natural power of the gods.
Furthermore, people in the surrounding villages said this:
“Is Mount Vediyaka on fire today? Is Mount Vediyaka burning today? Is Mount Vediyaka ablaze today?
Why has Mount Vediyaka become so exceedingly radiant today, as well as the mango grove and the brahmin village?”
They were moved with emotion and their hair stood on end.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabba devas:
"Dear Pañcasikha, it is difficult for one such as I to approach a Tathāgata who is absorbed in meditation, delighting in jhāna, and withdrawn in solitude."

"But if you, dear Pañcasikha, were to win the favor of the Blessed One first, then, dear one, having been won over by you first, we too would afterwards approach that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, to see him.

"Very well, venerable sir," replied Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabba deities, and having assented to Sakka, lord of the devas, he took his yellow-belved lute and went to Indasāla Cave. Having arrived there, he said:
“By this much, the Blessed One will be neither too far from me nor too close, and he will hear my voice,” thinking thus, he stood to one side.
1. The Verses Sung by Pañcasikha.
Standing to one side, Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabba deities, tuned his yellow beluva-wood lute and recited these verses concerning the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha,
the Arahants, and sensual pleasures: “I revere your father,
Bhaddā, O Timbarū’s daughter, Suriyavaccasā!
By whom you were born, O auspicious one,
the bringer of joy to me—
like the wind to those who are oppressed by heat, you are my beloved.
Just as water is dear to one who thirsts,
so is the Dhamma of the Arahants dear to Aṅgīrasa.
Like medicine for the sick,
like food for the hungry,
O Bhaddā, lead me to final Nibbāna.
Like water being poured into a pool of cool water,
a lotus pond endowed with the pollen of filaments.
Like an elephant tormented by the heat,
plunge into those breasts and belly;
like an elephant without a goad, [enter].
I have conquered with my *tuttatomara* weapon;
I do not understand the cause,
for I am merely equal to one with well-proportioned thighs.
I am possessed by greed,
my mind has been transformed;
I am unable to return [to my former state].
Like a lotus held by one with crooked hands,
O fair-thighed one, cling to me, O blessed lady;
cling to me, O you of lovely eyes!
Embrace me, O beautiful one; this is what I desire.
Alas, though I am but a small man!
Desire arose for her with curling hair;
she became manyfold,
like an offering to an Arhat.
Whatever merit I have performed toward such Arhats as these,
may all that, O lady beautiful in every limb, [be for your sake].
May it ripen together with her.
Whatever merit I have performed on this circle of the earth,
[may it ripen together with her].
May that merit of mine, O lady beautiful in every limb,
ripen together with yours,
just as the son of the Sakyas does through his meditative absorption.
One-pointed, prudent, and mindful—
the sage seeking the deathless—
him I praise, O you who shine like the sun.
Just as the Sage would rejoice upon attaining supreme enlightenment,
so too, O auspicious lady, may I rejoice.
I have attained the state of a woman.
Even if Sakka, the lord of the Thirty-three, were to grant me a boon;
Therefore, O Bhaddā, I would choose you as my bride;
such is my firm desire.
Like a sal tree in full bloom, I shall not wait long.
I pay homage and revere your father, O wise one,
whose offspring is such as this.
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabba devas:
"Pañcasikha, your lute tone blends with the vocal tone, and the vocal tone blends with the lute tone;
nor does your lute tone overstep the vocal tone, nor does the vocal tone overstep the lute tone."

“But when, Pañcasikha, were these verses—connected with the Buddha, connected with the Dhamma, connected with the Saṅgha, connected with the Arahants, and connected with sensual pleasures—composed by you?
“On one occasion, Bhante, the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, having just attained full enlightenment.
On that occasion, Bhante, there was a maiden named Bhaddā Suriyavaccasā, the daughter of Timbaru, the king of the gandhabbas, whom I desired.”
"Moreover, Bhante, that sister was in love with another;
she desired Mātali’s son named Sikhaddi.
Therefore, Bhante, when I could not obtain that sister by any means whatsoever,"
Then, taking my pale-wood lute, I went to the residence of Timbaru, the king of the gandhabbas. Having arrived,
I tuned the pale-wood lute and sang these verses concerning the Buddha,
the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the arahants, and sensual pleasures.
I revere your father, Bhaddā,
Timbaru, O daughter of the sun;
by him you were born as a virtuous woman.
The producer of my joy...
[as before] ...like a sal tree in full bloom, it will not last long.
To your father, O wise one,
I pay homage and offer salutation,
he whose offspring was such as this.
When this was said, Bhante, Bhaddā Suriyavaccasā said this to me:
“My dear sir, although I have not seen that Blessed One face-to-face, I have indeed heard of him while dancing in the Sudhamma assembly hall of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Since you, my dear sir, have praised that Blessed One, let there be a meeting for us today.”
“No, Bhante, there was no meeting with that sister;
nor has there been one since then.
2. Sakka’s Approach.
Then it occurred to Sakka, lord of the devas:
"Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabba devas, is exchanging greetings with the Blessed One, and the Blessed One is [exchanging greetings] with Pañcasikha.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabba devas:
“Pay homage for me, dear Pañcasikha, to the Blessed One, saying:
‘Venerable Sir, Sakka, lord of the devas, together with his ministers and his retinue, bows his head at the feet of the Blessed One.
“Very well, venerable sir,” replied Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabba deities, and having assented to Sakka, lord of the devas, he paid homage to the Blessed One.
“Bhante, Sakka, lord of the devas, together with his ministers and his retinue, bows his head at the feet of the Blessed One.
“May it be so, Pañcasikha; may Sakka, lord of the devas, together with his ministers and his retinue, be happy.
For gods, humans, asuras, nāgas, gandhabbas, and whatever other diverse beings there are, all desire happiness.”
And thus do Tathāgatas greet such highly esteemed yakkhas.
Having been greeted by the Blessed One, Sakka, lord of the devas, entered the Indasāla Cave, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood to one side.
The Tāvatiṁsa devas also entered the Indasāla Cave, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood to one side.
The gandhabba deity Pañcasikha also entered Indasāla Cave, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood to one side.

At that moment, the uneven parts of Indasāla Cave became level, the narrow parts became spacious, the darkness within the cave vanished, and light appeared, just as happens through the divine power of the devas.
Then the Blessed One said this to Sakka, lord of the devas:
“It is wonderful, venerable Kosiya! It is marvelous, venerable Kosiya! That you, who have so many duties and so much to do, should come here.
“Venerable sir, for a long time I have desired to approach the Blessed One to see him.
However, I have been occupied with various duties and tasks belonging to the Tāvatiṃsa devas; thus, I was unable to approach the Blessed One to see him.”
"Once, venerable sir, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Salaḷāgāra.
Then, venerable sir, I went to Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One.
Now at that time, venerable sir, the Blessed One was seated in a certain meditative absorption, and he was laughing."
And indeed, the attendant of the Great King Vessavaṇa was standing before the Blessed One, paying homage with her hands joined in reverence.
Then, Bhante, I said this to Bhūjati:
“Sister, please pay homage to the Blessed One for me, saying:
‘Venerable Sir, Sakka, lord of the devas, together with his ministers and retinue, bows his head at the feet of the Blessed One.
When this was said, Bhante, that bhujati said this to me:”
"It is not the right time, sir, to see the Blessed One;
the Blessed One is in seclusion.

"In that case, sister, when the Blessed One has emerged from that concentration, then pay homage to the Blessed One in my name, saying: [‘Venerable sir, the householder Citta pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet’]."
“Venerable sir, Sakka, lord of the devas, together with his ministers and his retinue, bows his head at the feet of the Blessed One.
Venerable sir, did that sister of mine pay homage to the Blessed One?
Does the Blessed One remember the words of that sister?”
“Sister, Lord of the Devas, she saluted me; I remember her words.
However, I was roused from that concentration by the sound of the Venerable One’s chariot wheel.
“Bhante, those deities who were born in the Tāvatiṃsa realm before us—I heard it directly from them and received it directly from their own mouths:”
‘When Tathāgatas arise in the world—Arahants, perfectly enlightened Buddhas—the divine hosts increase and the asura hosts diminish.

This, venerable sir, I have seen for myself: that since the Tathāgata has arisen in the world as an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, the divine hosts have increased and the asura hosts have diminished.
2.1. The Story of Gopaka.

"Right here in Kapilavatthu, Bhante, there was a daughter of the Sakyans named Gopikā. She had faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dhamma, and faith in the Saṅgha, and she practiced the precepts in their entirety.
Having outshone her female nature and developed the state of manhood, with the breakup of the body, after death, she was reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
She has entered into companionship with the Tāvatiṃsa devas and has attained the status of our son."
There too they know him thus:
“The young deva Gopaka, the young deva Gopaka.
Moreover, Bhante, there are three other bhikkhus who, having practiced the holy life under the Blessed One, have been reborn in an inferior gandhabba body.
Endowed with and possessed of those five strands of sensual pleasure, they attend upon us and provide us with service while enjoying themselves.
When they had come to attend upon us and were providing us with service, the young deity Gopaka rebuked them, saying:
“From what source, sirs, have you heard the Dhamma of that Blessed One?”
For I, though being a woman, having faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dhamma, and faith in the Saṅgha, and practicing the precepts in their entirety,
have outshone my femininity, developed masculinity, and with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a happy destination,
in a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, having attained the status of a son to Sakka, lord of the devas.
Here too, they know me thus:
“The young deva Gopaka, the young deva Gopaka.
But you, dear sirs, having practiced the holy life under the Blessed One, have been reborn in an inferior company of gandhabbas.
“Alas, friends, we have seen what is truly hard to see, in that we have seen our fellow practitioners reborn in the inferior company of the gandhabbas.

When they were thus reproved by the young deva Gopaka, two of those devas regained mindfulness right here in this very life and were reborn in the company of the Brahmapurohitas, while one deva remained addicted to sensual pleasures.
“I was a lay follower of the One with Vision...”
My name was Gopikā;
with deep faith in the Buddha and the Dhamma,
and with a clear heart, I served the Saṅgha.
By virtue of that very Buddha’s excellent Dhamma,
I am the son of Sakka, possessed of great majesty,
endowed with great radiance, reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Even here they know me as "Gopaka. Then,
O monks, I saw those who had been seen before,
dwelling there, having entered the company of the gandhabbas.
These disciples of Gotama,
and we ourselves who were formerly human beings,
have served you with food and drink.
Having clasped his feet in their own dwelling,
these venerable ones— whence did they turn their faces?—
have received the teachings of the Buddha.
For the Dhamma is to be realized within oneself,
well-taught by the One with Vision and awakened to;
indeed, I am one who attends upon you alone.
Having heard the well-spoken words of the Noble Ones,
I am the son of Sakka, possessed of great majesty and great radiance,
reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
But you, having approached the Best One and practiced the unsurpassed holy life,
have been reborn in an inferior body.
May rebirth not be contrary [to our wishes];
for we have indeed seen what is hard to see:
those who follow the same Dhamma fallen into a lower state.
"O beings who have entered the company of the gandhabbas,
come to serve the gods;
while I am living at home,"
Behold this distinction:
having been a woman, today I am a male god,
endowed with celestial sensual pleasures.
Urged on by that disciple of Gotama, they attained a sense of spiritual urgency upon meeting Gopaka:
"Come now, let us strive; let us exert ourselves!"
"Let us not become dependent on others";
of them, two applied themselves with energy,
recollecting the teachings of Gotama.
Having purified their minds right here,
they saw the danger in sensual pleasures; they [severed] the fetters and bonds of sensual desire.
The bonds of the Evil One are difficult to transcend.
Like a nāga that has severed its snares,
they have passed beyond the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
The Sainda gods together with Pajāpati,
all entered the Sudhamma assembly hall.
As they were seated there, [the following] approached them:
Seeing those heroes, free from passion, making themselves stainless,
Vāsava was moved to a sense of spiritual urgency in the midst of the host of gods, having surpassed them all.
"Those who have been reborn in a lower realm are now surpassing the Tāvatiṃsa devas";
having heard these words of one filled with spiritual urgency, he reflected upon them.
Then Gopaka addressed Vāsava in the midst [of the assembly]:
“There is a Buddha, O Lord of Men, in the world of humans;
he is known as the Sakyan Sage who has overcome all sensual desires.”
"Those sons of yours were devoid of mindfulness;
being exhorted by me, they regained their mindfulness.
Of those three, one here has entered the abode [of peace]."
Having attained mastery over the gandhabba realm,
and following the two paths to enlightenment, they,
with concentrated minds, hold even the gods in contempt.
In this exposition of the Dhamma such as this, no disciple there has any doubt;
he has crossed the flood and severed his uncertainty.
We pay homage to the Buddha, the Victor, the Lord of Men.
Having understood the Dhamma here,
they have attained distinction.
The Brahmā-purohita realm is their body;
two among them are distinguished.
For the sake of attaining that Dhamma,
“We have come, dear sir;
having been granted leave by the Blessed One,
we would ask a question, dear sir.”
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“For a long time this yakkha has been pure. Whatever question he asks me, he will ask only that which is beneficial, not that which is unbeneficial.
And whatever I answer when asked, he will quickly understand.”
Then the Blessed One addressed Sakka, lord of the devas, with a verse:
“Ask me, Vāsava, whatever question you desire in your mind.”
“Of each and every question,
I shall bring you to its end.
The first recitation section is finished.
Having been granted permission by the Blessed One, Sakka, lord of the devas, asked the Blessed One this first question: "Venerable sir, what fetters bind those gods,
humans, asuras, nāgas, gandhabbas, and others who exist in various bodies,

such that even though they think, 'May we dwell without enmity, without violence, without hostility, and without ill will— may we be free from enmity,' yet they still dwell with enmity, with violence, with hostility, and with ill will, being full of enmity?"
Thus Sakka, lord of the devas, asked the Blessed One a question.
Being thus questioned, the Blessed One answered his question:
"Lord of the devas, those fetters of envy and avarice—whether among devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, gandhabbas, or whatever other diverse classes of beings there may be—they [are bound by them]."

‘May we dwell without enmity, without weapons, without adversaries, without ill will, and free from enmity’—this is what they think, yet they dwell with enmity, with weapons, with adversaries, with ill will, and full of enmity.
Thus the Blessed One answered the question asked by Sakka, lord of the devas.
Delighted, Sakka, lord of the devas, rejoiced and approved of the Blessed One’s words.
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
My doubt is crossed over and my perplexity has vanished upon hearing the Blessed One’s answer to my question.
Thus Sakkadevānaminda, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, asked the Blessed One a further question:
“But, dear sir, what is the source of envy and avarice, what is their origin, what is their birth, what is their arising?
When what exists does envy and avarice come to be?
When what does not exist do envy and avarice not come to be?”
“Envy and avarice, Lord of the Devas, have what is dear and what is not dear as their source, as their origin, as their birth, and as their provenance.
When there is what is dear and what is not dear, envy and avarice arise;
when there is no more what is dear and what is not dear, envy and avarice do not exist.”
“But, dear sir, what is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, and what is the provenance of the pleasant and the unpleasant?
When what exists do the pleasant and the unpleasant come to be?
When what does not exist do the pleasant and the unpleasant not come to be?”
“O Lord of Devas, what is liked and what is disliked have desire as their source, desire as their origin, are born of desire, and arise from desire.
When there is desire, there is what is liked and what is disliked;
when there is no desire, there is nothing that is liked or disliked.”
“But, dear sir, what is the cause of desire, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its source?
When what exists does desire come to be?
When what does not exist does desire not come to be?”
“Desire, Lord of the Devas, has thought as its source, thought as its origin, thought as its birth, and thought as its cause;
when there is thought, desire comes to be;
when there is no thought, desire does not come to be.”
“But, dear sir, what is the source of applied thought (vitakka), what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance?
When what exists does applied thought come to be?
When what is absent does applied thought not come to be?”
“Thought, Lord of the Devas, has the proliferation of perceptions and notions as its source, its origin, its birth, and its provenance.
When there is the proliferation of perceptions and notions, thought arises;
when there is no proliferation of perceptions and notions, thought does not arise.”
“But in what way, dear sir, is a bhikkhu practicing the way that leads to the cessation of the formations of perceptions of proliferation?
2.2. The Meditation Subject of Feeling “O Lord of the Devas, I say that joy is twofold: [joy associated with the sensual] and [joy associated with the renunciate].”
There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
And regarding mental distress, O Lord of Devas, I speak of it as being twofold:
that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
“Furthermore, Lord of the Devas, I say that equanimity is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.
I also say, Lord of the Devas, that joy is of two kinds: that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated. Now, with reference to what was this said?”
In that regard, if one should know of a certain joy:
"When I indulge in this joy, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline," such a joy should not be indulged in.
In that regard, as for a certain joy...
‘While I am cultivating this kind of joy, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase’—such joy should be cultivated.
In that regard, whether it is accompanied by directed thought and evaluation or without directed thought and evaluation, those that are without directed thought and evaluation are more refined.
Thus, O Lord of Devas, I say that joy is of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
Thus, that which was said was said with reference to this.
"O Lord of Devas, I say that mental distress is of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated. Since this was said, with what in mind was it said?
In this regard, one should know that mental distress—
"If, by indulging in this grief, unwholesome states increase in me and wholesome states decline," such grief should not be indulged in.
In that regard, if one should know of a grief:
"By indulging in this grief, unwholesome states decline in me and wholesome states increase," such grief should be indulged in.

In this regard, whether it be accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, or without applied thought and without sustained thought—those that are without applied thought and without sustained thought are more excellent.

"O Lord of Devas, I say that mental displeasure is of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated"—this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
“Lord of the Devas, when I say that equanimity is of two kinds—that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated—what is it that I have said this in reference to?
In this regard, if one should know of a certain equanimity:
‘When I cultivate this equanimity, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,’ such equanimity is not to be cultivated.”
In this regard, if one should know of equanimity:
"When I cultivate this equanimity, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase," such equanimity should be cultivated.

In this regard, whether it be with applied thought and sustained thought, or without applied thought and without sustained thought—those that are without applied thought and without sustained thought are more excellent.
“Lord of the Devas, as for what was said by me— that equanimity is of two kinds, that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated—
it was said with reference to this.
For it is by practicing in this way, Lord of the Devas, that a bhikkhu has entered upon the way that leads to the cessation of the conceptual proliferations of perception.”
Thus the Blessed One, being asked the question by Sakka, lord of the devas, answered it.
Delighted, Sakka, lord of the devas, rejoiced and approved of the Blessed One’s words, saying:
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.”
“Having heard the Blessed One’s answer to my question, my doubt has been crossed over and my uncertainty has vanished.
Thus did Sakka, lord of the devas, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, ask the Blessed One a further question:
“But how, dear sir, does a bhikkhu practicing for restraint according to the Pātimokkha become one who practices for restraint according to the Pātimokkha?
“Lord of the Devas, I declare that bodily conduct is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.”
“O Lord of Devas, I declare that verbal conduct is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.
O Lord of Devas, I declare that search is also of two kinds.”
There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
"Lord of the Devas, I say that bodily conduct is of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated. This having been said, with reference to what was it said?
In this regard, one should know of a certain bodily conduct: [that it should be cultivated...]
"If, while practicing this bodily conduct, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline," such bodily conduct should not be practiced.
In that regard, whatever bodily conduct one should know:
"If I practice this bodily conduct, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase"—such bodily conduct should be practiced.
“Lord of the Devas, when I said that bodily conduct is twofold—
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated—
it was in reference to this that I spoke.”
“Lord of the Devas, I say that verbal conduct is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated. This is what was said; with reference to what was it said?

In this regard, if one should know of a certain verbal conduct: ‘When I cultivate this verbal conduct, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,’ such verbal conduct is not to be cultivated.”

In this regard, if one should know of a certain verbal conduct: "By practicing this verbal conduct of mine, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase," such verbal conduct should be practiced.
And, O Lord of Devas, I declare that verbal conduct is of two kinds:
that which is to be practiced and that which is not to be practiced.
Thus, that which was said—"O Lord of Devas, I declare that seeking is twofold:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated"—this being so, with reference to what was it said? With reference to what was this said?
In this regard, O Lord of Devas, if one should know of a pursuit: "When I pursue this, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline," such a pursuit should not be pursued.
But if one should know of a pursuit: "When I pursue this, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase," such a pursuit should be pursued.
I say, O Lord of Devas, that pursuit is twofold.
"Regarding what was said— that there is both that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated— it was said with reference to this.
For it is by practicing in this way, O Lord of Devas, that a bhikkhu is one who practices for the restraint of the Pātimokkha."
Thus the Blessed One, being asked a question by Sakka, lord of the devas, answered.
Delighted, Sakka, lord of the devas, rejoiced and approved of the Blessed One’s words:
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.”
“Having heard the Blessed One’s explanation of the question, my doubt is now crossed over and my uncertainty has vanished.
Thus, Sakka, lord of the devas, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, asked him a further question regarding the restraint of the sense faculties:
“But how, dear sir, does a bhikkhu practicing for the restraint of the sense faculties become one who is practicing?
“Lord of the Devas, I say that a form cognizable by the eye is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.”
“O Lord of Devas, I declare that sound cognizable by the ear is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.
O Lord of Devas, I declare that odor cognizable by the nose is also of two kinds:”
There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
O Lord of Devas, I declare that tastes cognizable by the tongue are of two kinds:
those that should be cultivated and those that should not be cultivated.
“O Lord of Devas, I declare that tactile objects cognizable by the body are of two kinds:
those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated.
O Lord of Devas, I declare that mental phenomena cognizable by the mind are also of two kinds.”
“...that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
When this was said, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Venerable sir, I understand in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken in brief in this way:”

“Venerable sir, whatever kind of form cognizable by the eye, when indulged in, leads to the increase of unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome states—such a form cognizable by the eye should not be indulged in.

But whatever kind of form cognizable by the eye, venerable sir, when indulged in, leads to the decline of unwholesome states and the increase of wholesome states—such a form cognizable by the eye should be indulged in.
And whatever kind of sound cognizable by the ear, venerable sir, when indulged in…” [and so on].
For one who indulges in a scent cognizable by the nose… for one who indulges in a flavor cognizable by the tongue… for one who indulges in a tangible object cognizable by the body…

“Venerable sir, when one cultivates a mental object cognizable by the mind such that unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, such a mental object cognizable by the mind should not be cultivated.

But, venerable sir, when one cultivates a mental object cognizable by the mind such that unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase, such a mental object cognizable by the mind should be cultivated.
It is in this way, venerable sir, that I understand in detail the meaning of what was stated by the Blessed One in brief.”
“Crossed over is my doubt, and my perplexity has vanished, having heard the Blessed One’s answer to my question.
Thus, Sakka, lord of the devas, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, asked the Blessed One a further question:
“Are all recluses and brahmins, dear sir, of one-sided views, of one-sided virtue, of one-sided desires, and of one-sided attachments?”
“Indeed, Lord of the Devas, not all recluses and brahmins are of one-sided views, one-sided conduct, one-sided desires, and one-sided attachments.
“But why, dear sir, are not all recluses and brahmins of one-sided views, one-sided conduct, one-sided desires, and one-sided attachments?
“Because, Lord of the Devas, the world consists of many elements and diverse elements.”
“In this world with its many elements and manifold elements, whatever element beings adhere to, they adhere to that very thing with persistence and attachment, and having adhered to it, they declare:
‘Only this is true, anything else is false.
Therefore, not all recluses and brahmins are of one-sided views, one-sided conduct, one-sided desires, or one-sided attachments.”

“Are all ascetics and brahmins, dear sir, indeed those who have reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate consummation?

“All ascetics and brahmins, Lord of Devas, are not those who have reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate consummation.

“But why, dear sir, are not all ascetics and brahmins those who have reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate consummation?”

“Those monks, O Lord of the Devas, who are liberated through the destruction of craving, have reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and achieved the ultimate consummation.
Therefore, not all recluses and brahmins have reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and achieved the ultimate consummation.
Thus the Blessed One answered the question asked by Sakka, the Lord of the Devas.
Satisfied, Sakka, lord of the devas, rejoiced and approved of the Blessed One’s words, saying:
“So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Sugata!
Having heard the Blessed One’s explanation of the question, my doubt has been crossed over and my uncertainty has vanished.”
Thus, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, movement is a disease, movement is a tumor, movement is a dart; movement drags this person along toward the production of this or that state of existence.
Therefore, this person undergoes high and low states.”
“Bhante, those questions for which I could not even find an opportunity to ask other recluses and brahmins outside this fold have been answered by the Blessed One.
Furthermore, that shaft of doubt and perplexity which had lain latent within me for a long time has been extracted by the Blessed One.
“Devānaminda, do you recall asking these same questions of other recluses and brahmins?”
“I recall, venerable sir, having asked these same questions of other ascetics and brahmins.
“But how, Devānaminda, did they answer? If it is not troublesome for you, please speak.
“It would not be troublesome for me, venerable sir, were the Blessed One himself seated there, or one like the Blessed One.”
“In that case, Lord of the Devas, speak.

“Venerable sir, regarding those ascetics and brahmins whom I consider to be forest-dwellers who frequent remote lodgings, I approach them and ask these questions. When questioned by me, they do not manage to answer; failing to answer, they instead question me in return:
‘What is the name of the venerable one?’”
When questioned by them, I replied:
“I am indeed, sir, Sakka, lord of the devas.
They then questioned me further:
"But, Lord of the Devas, what deed did the Venerable One perform to reach this state?
To them I teach the Dhamma exactly as I have heard it and mastered it.
They are satisfied with that alone, saying:
“We have seen Sakka, lord of the devas, and he has answered us exactly what we asked.
In every way, they become my disciples, but I am not theirs.
“However, Bhante, I am a disciple of the Blessed One—a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, and headed for full enlightenment.”
2.5. Discourse on the Attainment of Joy “Sire, Lord of the Devas, do you recall having previously experienced such a feeling, such an attainment of joy?
“I do recall, venerable sir, having previously experienced such a feeling, such an attainment of joy.”
“But how, Lord of the Devas, do you recall having previously experienced such a gain of happiness and a gain of joy?
“Formerly, venerable sir, there occurred a battle arrayed between the devas and the asuras.
In that battle, venerable sir, the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated.”
“Venerable sir, after I had won that battle and emerged victorious, this thought occurred to me:
‘Now, both the divine vitality and the asura vitality—both these shall be enjoyed by the devas.
Yet, venerable sir, that attainment of knowledge and that attainment of joy of mine was accompanied by punishment and accompanied by weapons.”
It does not lead to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to peace, nor to direct knowledge, nor to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna.
But this attainment of wisdom, this attainment of joy, which I have gained, Bhante, upon hearing the Dhamma from the Blessed One—
"It is not within the domain of punishment or the domain of weapons; it leads to utter disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
"But, Lord of Devas, what purpose do you perceive that leads you to proclaim such an attainment of wisdom and such an attainment of joy?"
“Bhante, it is seeing six reasons that I proclaim such an attainment of rapture and an attainment of joy.
While remaining right here,
even though I have become a deity:”
"And my life has been regained;
know this, dear sir.
It is seeing this first benefit, venerable sir, that I proclaim such an attainment of happiness and an attainment of joy."
Having passed away from the celestial realms and relinquished my superhuman lifespan,
I shall enter a womb without confusion.
"Wherein my mind finds delight.
It is seeing this second benefit, Bhante, that I declare such an attainment of inspiration and an attainment of joy.
Thus, to one of undeluded wisdom—
Delighting in the teaching, I shall dwell in the monastery;
I will live by the right method,
clearly comprehending and fully mindful.
"Venerable sir, seeing this third reason for its benefit, I declare such an attainment of rapture and an attainment of joy:
'If, while I am conducting myself according to the Dhamma,
full enlightenment should come to pass...'"
"I shall dwell as one who has fully understood;
this very day it will come to an end.
Venerable sir, seeing this fourth benefit, I declare such an attainment of happiness and an attainment of joy.
Having cast off this human body and abandoned the human lifespan,
I shall become a deva once again.
He is supreme in the world of the gods.
Venerable sir, seeing this fifth benefit, I proclaim such an attainment of inspiration and an attainment of joy.
Those gods are even more sublime.
The glorious Akaniṭṭha realm;
when my final existence occurs,
that shall be my dwelling place.
"Venerable sir, seeing this sixth reason for its benefit, I declare such an attainment of feeling, such an attainment of joy.
Venerable sir, it is seeing these six reasons for its benefit that I declare such an attainment of feeling, such an attainment of joy.
One whose intention is not yet fulfilled..."
Full of doubt and indecisive,
I wandered for a long time,
seeking the Tathāgata.
Regarding those ascetics whom I consider to be living in seclusion,
I think of them as being fully awakened ones.
I go to attend upon you [to ask]:
"How is there fulfillment? How is there failure?"
Thus questioned, they could not provide an answer regarding the path and the ways of practice.
Then, when they recognized me—
Sakka, the lord of the gods, has come;
he asks me this very question:
"By doing what did you attain this?"
To them I teach the Dhamma as I have heard it from people;
by that they become glad at heart.
And: “We have seen Vāsava!
And when I beheld the Buddha, the one who carries me across doubt;
Today I am free from fear,
having paid homage to the Fully Awakened One,
the slayer of the arrow of craving.
I pay homage to the Buddha, the peerless one, the Great Hero,
the Buddha who is a kinsman of the Sun.
Whatever we do for Brahmā,
O dear sir, together with the gods—
that today we shall do for you.
Come now, let us make peace with you.
You alone are the perfectly awakened one;
you are the unsurpassed Teacher.
"In the world with its gods,
there is no one who is your equal.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabbas:
“You have been of great service to me, dear Pañcasikha, in that you were the first to inspire confidence in the Blessed One.
Because you first inspired confidence in him, we subsequently approached that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for an audience.
I shall establish you in your ancestral position; you shall become a king of the gandhabbas. And I give you Bhaddā Suriyavaccasā, for she is the one you desired.”
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, touched the earth with his hand and three times uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!”
"Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One!
And while this exposition was being spoken, the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose in Sakka, lord of the devas:
"Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation."
And for eighty thousand other deities;
thus, those questions which were asked by Sakka, lord of the devas, have been answered by the Blessed One.
Therefore, this exposition is indeed designated by the name "Sakka-ppañha" (The Questions of Sakka).
The Sakkapañha Sutta is finished; it is the eighth.
